speechtext: Mr. NESBITT moved that the Select Standing Committee on Railways have leave to sit during the sessions of the House, as recommended in the report of the Committee.

Are we trying to revive such resolution passed before the committee this morning. We have only one Bill to deal with and as the next meeting of the committee is called for 10 o'clock instead of 11 o'clock on Tuesday next when the House sits there is no need of this motion.
It was recommended by the committee on the 16th of May.
Oh, that was on the eve-of adjournment, and when there were a lot of Bills to be disposed of, but there is only one Bill before us now.
I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) that this motion is absolutely unnecessary under existing conditions. The work before the committee is not heavy now.
The work is not very heavy, but the talk is.

That-one Bill before the committee will have to be carefully considered and it will probably be opposed by nearly all the members of the House when they understand it. I can well understand that certain interests would want this motion to pass, but they are not the interests of the people. If it does pass it will have the effect of compelling members to neglect their duties in the committee or else neglect their duties in this House. This Bill refers to a charter that has been absolutely dead for three years and that never was heard of in the House of Commons until the day before adjournment after we had been in session for six months.
Did this Bill come from the Senate?

This Bill came from the Senate, but they must have been late

in introducing it in the Senate or else it would have got to this House before it did. It is a Bill entirely in the interests of a private corporation, 'and in view of the urgent public business before the House it can very well wait until next session.

The Bill could have passed the Committee this morning, as the great majority of the committee desired, but upon the request of the hon. member for East Grey and others we consented to allow the Bill to stand over in order that those who might possibly have any interest in opposing it should be notified. We did not touch upon the merits of the Bill this morning.
The hon. member (Mr. Devlin) says the majority of the committee were seized of the Bill this morning, and prepared to pass it, but now he says they did not even consider the merits.
What I said was that the Bill was fully discussed and the majority of the committee quite prepared to pass it, but now these gentlemen opposite want to kill it entirely.

We are not endeavouring to kill the Bill but we are pointing out that the committee has adjourned until Tuesday next at ten o'clock, which is an hour before the sitting of the House, and we think there is plenty of time to consider the Bill, without passing this motion.
The hon. member for East Grey will himself speak for an hour against the Bill.
Not at all.
We will get to eleven o'clock when the House meets and then the committee will have to rise.

I do not think I spoke more than five minutes on the Bill this morning. The consideration of the Bill was adjourned in view of the fact that the committee were notified that the city council of Montreal and the board of trade desired to be heard and had no notice, and that the R. & 0. Co'y had their representatives before the committee saying that only late yesterday did they receive intimation that the Bill would be considered to-day, and they desired to consider carefully whether or not it would prejudicially affect their interests. It is for that reason we asked delay.

It is not a public Bill and the public interest can in no way be affected. The Bill came to us from the Senate and has been before parliament for a considerable time. In view of the attitude some hon. gentlemen assume Mr. LANCASTER.
towards the Bill it would seem to me that in the hour between 10 o'clock and 11 o'clock no progress could be made. It is to give those who oppose the Bill the fullest opportunity to be heard that this motion has been made.

The government has
thought it vitally important to call special morning sittings of the House for the consideration of an important public measure, and under these circumstances it is unfair that members of this House should be prevented attending to their duty here by obtruding on them the consideration of a private Bill in the committee. There is ample time to consider this Bill between ten and eleven in the morning and between two and three in the afternoon, if necessary, when the House is not in session. As a member of the Railway Committee it is unfair that I should be compelled to neglect my important duties in this House with reference to a measure in which my constituents are deeply interested, simply because I am forced to attend a meeting of a committee.

The Railway Committee is composed of practically nearly all the members of the House, and this motion would compel them to neglect their duty in the committee or to be absent when a public measure of vital importance is being considered in the House. The Minister of the Interior told us last night that many measures of great public importance would not pass this session because of insufficient time. He told us that the Grain Bill which was introduced in the interests of the farmers would have to stand aside, that the Bank Act, and important amendments to the Railway Act would not be allowed to go through this session for the same reason.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member says that I stated that these measures would not be allowed to go through this session because of press of business he misunderstood me entirely. I said that these measures weTe claiming the pressing atten-tion_ of the House, but had been compelled to give way to the discussion of the matter now before the House. I did not convey the impression that they would not be dealt with later on.

The Minister of the Interior said that these w^re more important than the matter brought up by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, and we all understand him to say they would not b-e able fo get through this session. The minister said that the Bank Act would not go through because of want of time, and so we had to pass an interim Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I stated the fact with regard to the Bank Act, but Hansard will

bear me out that I did not convey any impression such as the hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) has referred to.
Does the Minister of the Interior think that the Grain Act, the Bank Act, and the amendments to the Railway Act, are less important than this private Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not considered ihat question at all.
Will the minister say that we should give'precedence to this private Bill before these important measures?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not thought of that.
Such a proposition as this is entirely unreasonable under existing conditions, and it should not be forced on us.

' Unfortunately Ontario conditions are such that no fairly comparable figures can be made up. No flocks approaching in size those shown by the Ohio tables are to be found. in another case prices of oats are quoted in the hon. member's inquiry in such a manner as to apparently show that the United States prices range from 27 to 35 cents per bushel, while the Canadian prices range from 28 to 36 cents per bushel. I have noticed that some days ago certain cases supposed to be cholera were quarantined below Quebec, and I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture whether he has any information on the subject that he is 'able to communicate to the House so as to relieve the anxiety of the people of the country in regard to this dreaded disease.

The cases referred to were somewhat suspicious, and the physician in charge detained them for separate examination. A 'bacteriological examination has been made, and the doctors have declared that the disease is not cholera, so that there is no case of quarantine at present.

I rise to a question of privilege. On the night before last, when I was not in the House, the Minister of Public Works made reference to me personally in connection with some correspondence addressed to the Minister of Finance by the Riordon Paper Company, in which I happen to hold some stock. Considering the statements made in the House by my hon friend the Minister of Finance, I am rather surprised that he should have allowed this correspondence to be used in this way. On the 3rd of February the Minister of Finance said this in this House with regard to correspondence on the subject of reciprocity:
With regard to correspondence respecting reciprocity with the government there is practically none. Many people made representations to the government but beyond a polite *acknowledgment of their letters, there is no correspondence. In some cases these representations, although not marked confidential, are such as I would hardly feel free to bring down because they relate to particular interests that might be, or thought they might be affected by the negotiations, and I could not without their consent publish these.
This matter was discussed a good many times in the House, and I understood that the Minister of Finance was firm in the position that this correspondence was private correspondence.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that this correspondence was brought down months ago and is on the files of the House?
I was not aware of that.
It was from the files that I got it.
Even now I do not understand how that could be done after the remarks made by the Minister of Finance.
It was not brought down.
It was, months ago.
Was all the private correspondence referred to by the Minister of Finnace brought down?

There was no private correspondence from anybody brought down -no letter marked private, or which in its nature was private. I do not remember the particular letter referred to. I happened to be engaged when the Minister of Public Works was speaking, and beyond some reference to that company in which the hon. gentleman is interested I did not notice any reference to the letter. But I can only say that if there was anything in that letter intended to be private, I would not have brought it down. I did not give it to the Minister of Public Works. I presume that he must have got it from the public files. I do not know when it was brought down, but up to this moment I have not heard that there has been any objection on the part of the company to its being brought down.

I have no objection to this correspondence being brought down at all. I did not know that it was on file, and I would like the Minister of Public Works to tell me when it was placed on the table of the House and why that was done.

I do not know why it was brought down. It was brought with a great deal of other correspondence. I happened to see it with a letter from my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) referring to a communication from a large lumber company urging a reduction in the United States duty on shingles, and with letters from people dealing in hay, which were laid on the table of the House a good many months ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me, I will answer the question why it was brought down. It was brought down in answer to a demand of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), if I am not mistaken, that all correspondence on this subject should be brought down, and all

the correspondence which either was not marked private or was not, from its very nature obviously intended to be private, has been brought down.

That, I take it, is only another way of saying that the minister has brought down just what he thought fit to bring down, and nothing more. I have no objection to these letters being brought down, but it seems to me the minister ought to have some general rule in these matters and not apply special rules to suit the purposes of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What rule would the hon. gentleman suggest?
I think that either everything not marked ' private ' should be brought down or nothing should be brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Can my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) tell me of any case of which he complains? I do not think that in the case of the letter from this company in which the hon. gentleman is said to be interested, that the manager who wrote it ever complained, and I do not think he would complain of our action. There was nothing private in the letter, nor anything to indicate that it was intended to be private.	.
I quite understand that, but it seems to me that all the letters should be treated alike.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I received letters from my colleagues on this side, which though not marked private, were toy their nature manifestly intended as private, and these I did not bring down.

In other words, the government brings down such correspondence as suits its convenience. However, I do not wish the House to think that I have any objection to the bringing down of these letters, or that there is anything in them that might not be made public. But I wish to say, in the first place, I have nothing to do personally with the active management of this compnay. I have so much work to do here that I have not tried to take part in the other. So, I found it necessary to telephone to Montreal to find out regarding these letters. I find that, in the first place, the statement of the Minis-
Mr. FIELDING
ter of Public Works, that this company urged very strongly that a reciprocal arrangement should be entered into, is not in accordance with the letter. This company has a large output of sulphite pulp, and it so happens that the ordinary terms ' pulp ' and ' paper' as used do not include sulphite pulp, and this company simply wished to bring that point to the attention of the government in order that, if any treaty were made with the United States, the wording should be such as to cover sulphite pulp. This company is not a political company nor a Tory concern: it is a Canadian company. And if there were to toe an arrangement with the United States they simply wished to bring proper information to the attention of the government. Now, the Minister of Public Works has said that he has been told that it would mean $90,000 to this company. It is easy for the minister to get up and make that statement. But there can be no foundation for it. This company will certainly derive some advantage, but the information the minister gives, if he has not got it from his inner consciousness must have been given him by somebody who knew nothing about the matter. It is utterly impossible that there should be such a benefit to the company. Further, the minister says that this will come about if the proposed arrangement goes into effect. The pulp and paper clauses depends on the will of the provinces, as this parliament has no power to put this into effect. It is true that if it comes into force immediately, pulp wood from private lands will be affected. But it is well known^ that the greater part of the business done by all these companies is done on Crown lands.
Now, with regard to the hon. minister's (Mr. Pugsley's) personal reference and insinuations regarding myself. I can only say that I am opposed to this reciprocity pact, because I think it is a bad thing for Canada; I am opposed to it on principle. And I extend to the hon. minister my sincere sympathy and pity that he seems utterly unable to understand how any one can regard a public question from any other point of view than the effect upon his own pocket.

I am very glad to get the information which my hon. friend has given to the House that he has nothing to do with the active management of this company. Otherwise he would know of the very considerable quantities of pulp and paper which this company is to-day shipping to the United States and would realize the great benefits which would accrue to the company if pulp and paper were admitted free to the United States. I presume he knows something of the details of the work of the company.
Does not the hen. gentleman think that my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) knows as much about the subject as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley)?

The Minister of Public Works has had the very great advantage of reading the admirable letter written by the manager of the Eiordan Paper Mills Company. And I wish to congratulate the hon. gentleman (Mr. Perley) being, as he says simply a stockholder of the company, upon the excellent ability and excellent judgment of the young man who is now in the position of general manager of the Eiordan Company. I do not know that there is any man ;n this country or in the United States engaged in the manufacture of pulp and paper who is more qualified
If we are going to have a debate on this sub
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has heard enough?

I am not through yet. I tell the hon. gentleman that if he and the gentlemen associated with him in this parliament, and associated with him politically in the province of New Brunswick, would produce the correspondence and the records which some of them at all events have in their possession, there would. be disclosed to the people of this country and to this House as great a conspiracy against myself as ever was concocted against any public man in this country. If there is anything the hon. gentleman can find out he is welcome to it.

I think perhaps the hon. gentleman will not be so entirely satisfied with the statement of facts with regard to that as he professes to be at the present time. I rose for the reason that the hon. gentleman made a most uncalled for insinuation against the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley), and then was proceeding to deal with a matter that was absolutely irrelevant to the question raised by the member for Argenteuil, dealing with the internal affairs of the Eiordan Paper Company. Minister of Public Works.	.

I would remind the House that the debate is very irregular at this time.
I was replying to the hon. member for Argenteuil, and I was saying that the letter-

When a question of privilege is raised the custom of the House is that the member raising it has the floor. I allowed the Minister of Public Works to speak because I thought he was making some personal explanation. Beyond that, the debate was irregular, because there is nothing before the House.

Before the orders of the day are proceeded with I would like to ask again when the report on the Sorel affair will be laid on the table of the House. It is required for the purpose of discussion. I do not know if my hon. friend has acquired the habit of withholding documents.

I told my hon. friend yesterday that Mr. Boyle, the inspector of agencies, has made an inspection in Sorel and has been there for some time. He has not yet put in his report; he is away from town just now, and is expected back at the beginning of next week, when he will make his report forthwith.

speechtext: CROCKET (York, N.B.) Before you leave the Chair, I desire to call attention to a matter which has been investigated in the Public Accounts Committee, and which I think deserves the serious consideration of the House. I refer to the contract which was awarded by the Public Works Department to the Marine Dredging and Construction Company for dredging ai the Gaspereau river, New Brunswick. I do not know whether this is another case of a conspiracy to destroy the character of the Minister of Public Works, but I leave it to the members of the House to judge after they have heard the evidence that was adduced before the Public Accounts Committee.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend tell me the date of that investigation?

speechtext:
I see the minister has been examining the evidence since he came Mr. SPEAKER.
into the House, so he is just as familiar with the facts as I am. The evidence shows that this contract was illegally awarded to the Maritime Dredging and Construction Company, which I think the members of the House are aware is owned and controlled by the minister's personal and political friends, Mr. George McAvity and Mr. John A. Moore. The contract was not only awarded illegally to that company, in contravention of the law, but under it the sum of $33,900 was paid to the Maritime Dredging and Construction Company for work which the resident district engineer in charge of the work reported was of no value. Now this transaction began, so far as the records of the department disclose, in the month of July, 1908. Previous to that date there had been two reports sent to the Public Works Department upon the proposed work. One of these reports was made by Mr. Day, the resident engineer of the department, on the. 13th day of May, 1903, when that officer estimated that the cost of the proposed work, which was a channel giving twelve feet at low water, would be $168,000. Mr. Day based his estimate on 20 cents a cubic yard. The matter rested then until 1907, when, on the 5th of March, Mr. Geoffrey Stead, Mr. Day's successor as resident engineer, made another report, estimating that the work would require about 330,000 cubic yards to be dredged, costing, at 20 cents, $66,000.

maintopic: WAYS AND MENAS-DREDGING AT GASPEREAU HARBOUR.
speechtext: What is the date of that?

maintopic: WAYS AND MENAS-DREDGING AT GASPEREAU HARBOUR.
speechtext:
March 5, 1907. There the matter rested until the 15th of July, 1908, when the general elections of that year were approaching. Then we find it suddenly revived by this direction from the deputy minister to the then engineer:
Kindly let me know as soon as possible just what quantity of urgent dredging is required at the Gaspereau river.
The resident engineer was accordingly asked by the chief engineer for his estimate of the quantity, on the 16th of July, and on the 17th of July, Mr. Stead sent this telegram to the chief engineer:
In reply to your telegram at Gaspereau river, a cut to give six feet at low water through bar necessitating removing 48,000 cubic yards, barge measurement, is most urgently required. Basin, 350 feet long, 200 feet wide; at wharfs also very necessary, requiring
14,000	cubic yards barge measurement, of dredging.
On the 20th of July the acting deputy minister, Mr. Hunter, instructed the secretary of the department to have advertisements sent out calling for tenders for dredging at Gaspereau river, at Buctouche beach and at Buctouche harbour and at Point du Chene in the province of New Brunswick.

The advertisements issued on the 28th and bears date the 28th of January calling for tenders for dredging at these places. On the 31st of July, three days after the issue of the advertisement calling for tenders, we have this extraordinary telegram received by the chief engineer at Otawa:
Chatham, N.B., July 31, 1908.
To the Chief Engineer, .
Dept, of Public Works, Ottawa, Ont.

In 1900 I had the honour of being elected as representative of the county of Westmoreland in this House. At that time, and for some years previous, the locality of the harbour of Baie Verte and Port Elgin had claimed the attention of previous representatives of that county, and the condition of those harbours and of the approaches thereto were matters of deep concern. to the people interested. Under a previous government an attempt was made to afford transportation facilities by the erection of a ballast wharf in the open bay at Baie Verte, lying between Baie Verte and Port Elgin, between the streams known as the Baie Verte stream or creek and the stream known as the Gaspereau, which flows down by the village of Port Elgin. This ballast wharf was built there as a sort of loading wharf. There was no possibility of small steamers approaching the landings by the Eiver Gaspereau, or up in the river of Gaspereau, or to approach near the village of Baie Verte. A former government, some twenty-five years ago, constructed this ballast, or load landing wharf, right out in the open, and it was necessary to scow out to that landing. It was thought that they could make improvements affording reasonable transportation and shipping facilities for the people of those communities. That had utterly failed, in fact it had been so constructed that soon afterwards it became a little restive in its position, and began wandering around the bav, and people were afraid that if they put anything upon it it might go adrift.
So after a time it became obsolete as affording shipping facilities. Then the people of Port Elgin thought it was important that dredging should be done, so that vessels drawing at least 12 or 14 feet of water might have access to the wharfs, and to the mills and other industrial establishments in that community. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the village of Port Elgin, while small, has many industrial establishments. In 1903, when the engineer of the department went there to inquire into the matter, it had five sawmills and four fish-curing and fish-smoking industries. At that time it was struggling to be recognized as one of the industrial centres of the county of Westmoreland. To-day it has reached a measure of its ambition, and is steadily improving and developing. Now those were the conditions. It was necessary to afford these facilities for the people, and in 1901, at the first session of parliament, when Mr. Tarte was Minister of Public Works, I brought the matter to his notice, and as a result of my conference with him, he sent officers of his department to make a survey. In February and March, I think, of 1901, Mr. Day, an officer connected with the Department of Public Works in the province of New Brunswick, under the direction of his chief, Mr. Shewan, went to Port Elgin, and there, during the winter months, on the ice, made a thorough survey and borings to ascertain the dredging that would be necessary. The report of that engineer is before this House, and it shows what dredging was necessary. There was at the very mouth of the river a baT, 1,200 to 1,500 feet in width, that would have to be dredged out.
A channel was necessary that they might make use of that and then they have penetrated that bar in order to reach the main channel to Gaspereaux river. He pointed out the necessity of widening the channel of the river and then going up to what is known as the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island drawbridge. There is a railway bridge across the stream, which bridge was supposed to have a draw, which did have a draw and which has one now, but it was necessary that the river should be widened and deepened in order to reach the basin where are the wharfs, private and public, and also to reach the Hickman & Co. mills.

Eight feet. At that time there w'as a little water in the basin at low water, but in the river there was from 4 to 6 feet of water at low water. Here were milling establishments, here j were fishing establishments which requir-

Since that time the growth of business in that locality has been large, a number of fishing establishments have been erected-, and yet it will be noted that year by year the numbers of vessels sailing in and out of the port of Port Elgin has decreased. It was alleged by the prominent citizens of that locality that something would have to be done, that the river was filling up with sawdust from mills up the stream, and that it, would -be necessary to remove these obstructions which had- grown year by year, and were the cause, as they alleged, of decreasing the shipping in thait port. Come to the point,

I am answering my hon. friend's complaint about the language I made use of. If he complains^ of the expression ' diseased imagination,' 1 may put it a little more mildly, and say that he is affected by a brain storm.
It is better to allow all personal allusions to remain outside of the debate.

I think my language has been moderate, and there is no one more desirous than I am that decorum in debate, that manliness and courtesy, should prevail in this House. But this is a matter of which I have a personal knowledge as a representative of the people, and when statements are made before the House in order that a wrong impression may go abroad, I feel it my duty to characterize them in .terms that are mild, having regard to the utterances of the hon. gentleman. Because I have suffered from such insinuations, I know just what is the effect of insinuations against public men, whether they are uttered in this House or out of it, as I know what the effect is with respect to the character of men and women when made even by a shake of the head. I would prefer that men should stand up in their places and manfully speak out what they have in their minds, rather than indulge in these insinuations and inferences. -
Dont be too hard on the Minister of Public Works.

I do not think it is necessary for my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) to interject himself into this debate; we

have enough unpleasantness about it now. Bear in mind that the instructions given by the officials of the department to the Maritime Dredging Company were that they should merely do the lesser work, that is in connection with the reports of Mr. Stead. They went there and faithfully performed their work, they earned every dollar that was paid to them, and indeed, as I am informed, they lost by reason of the dangers incidental to the situation of the work.
There is no evidence of that.
There is evidence, the statement made on March 10. On my honour as a member of this House, they lost their tug in a storm, and declined to go *back because of the dangerous conditions there.
There is absolutely no evidence.

Now my hon. friend has said that this contract was illegal, and in violation of the Public Works Act. I am bound to say that that is not a correct statement of the case. This was a work of urgency, a work of necessity that justified the sending of dredges there. Has the public treasury of Canada suffered in any way? Men are engaged to do woTk that is absolutely necessary, and upon the best terms possible. How? Not by any hole and corner arrangement between the Minister of Public Works and the contractors, but on public competition throughout Canada. The amount was fixed, and I understand that the 90 cents which was paid applied only to a portion of the work, and that only 60 cents was paid on another portion. I would be glad to see the estimate of the engineer adhered to, if it could be, 20 cents per cubic yard. I can only say that the engineer must have had in his mind dredging within the river banks and within the harbour basin. The bottom of that harbou'r and of that basin consisted largely of silt and sawdust, and sand and clay, and perhaps he thought that his work would all be of that character. But we must remember that the work out on the bar, out in the open roadstead, was of an entirely different class, that it involved greater dangers and greater risks; and I venture to say that because of that fact there were no lower tenders, and because of that fact there were no owners of dredging plants who were disposed to engage in the work. I have understood, and think I can state it as a fact, that since then an earnest attempt has been made to find suitable dredging plant to go on and engage in that woTk. If it is to be put up to tender again, that bar being out of the question, the dredging of that channel through this
bar across the harbour mouth, out in the open bay and roadstead, being finished, 1 think the work can be done much more cheaply within the river and within the harbour and basin.
Now I want to emphasize this fact. There are large industrial establishments there to-day that are handicapped. The Hickman Milling Co., Limited, is a concern doing a very large business. In the manufacture of deals they are compelled, and will be compelled, to avail themselves of the transportation facilities afforded by the railways from Port Elgin to Cape Tormentine, where shipments are made in steamers from the government pier to the ports in Great Britain. Incidental to the manufacture of deals-and there are other mills there, four I believe-incidental to the manufacture of deals for the markets of Great Britain, there is produced a quantity of small scantlings, boards and laths.
These must find markets elsewhere than in Great Britain. Despite the fact that there has been a duty of $1,25 a thousand on lumber going into the United States these people have been obliged to send their surplus in the United States and although they have open to them the market of Newfoundland and the local markets of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, while they avail themselves of all of them, they are still obliged to send a great proportion of their lumber to the United States much to their disadvantage. They are obliged to transport that from Port Elgin by rail at additional expense to Sackvilie and Cape Tormentine and there ship to Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, and United States ports. Would it not be an incalculable advantage to them if this dredging were completed? They would be enabled to have their schooners that could sail into the ports of the United States come to their wharf, take in their cargo, and they would thereby save expense and I am glad to say that with the prospect of a reciprocity treaty whereby lumber will go free into the United States and whereby they would have an open door they would have an additional advantage. Mr. Speaker, being .a member of the Public Accounts Committee and having been present during this investigation, I feel that I would like to say a few words on this motion moved by my hon. friend from York, New Brunswick (Mr. Crocket). 'St. John Telegraph ' so as to convert it from a Conservative newspaper to a newspaper working in the interests of the hon. member of Westmoreland. Of a contract which was not let.

Moore went to Montreal, purchased a second-hand dredge from the Gilbert people and went straight back to Gaspereau, and on August 4th he is at work on this contract at ninety cents a yard. Moore and Loggie and others are walking around the maritime provinces with money they robbed from the people of this country.

The hon. member's recollection is very bad. It does not matter whether it is $65,000 or $5,000, if it is wrongfully given and they have succeed-in robbing the country the principle is exactly the same. In the Public Works Department we have brought up matters of this kind where there is no question in the eyes of the people of this country that public robbery has been going on, and the Minister of Public Works has taken no steps to stop it. We brought up, for example, the amount expended for the sawdust wharf, where the difference between $700 and $5,000 was robbed from the people of this country through the neglect or influence of the Minister of Public Works, I do not know which, but by one way or Mr. REID (Grenville).
the other, either by the minister in not attending to his business or else by giving this man the option of getting this $4,300.
Would it not be fair for the hon. gentleman to say that the large part of the difference was repaid to the government for a part of the property sold?

The way it was repaid was that when the Minister of Public Works was in a hole in the eyes of the people of this country he sent down for the Loggie Dredging Company, and they came up and paid $3,700 for a part of it and it has never been used since.

The hon. gentleman is speaking absolutely without evidence when he says that I sent down for the Loggies. There is not a particle of evidence of that, and if we can truly characterize a gentleman who keeps so far away from the truth as my hon. friend by saying that he has a diseased imagination, I think his imagination is even more diseased than that of the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket).

If I have a diseased imagination the Minister of Public Works must have a diseased brain when he allows such rascality to go on in his department. He tells us he did not send for Loggie. Did he not bring Loggie here as a witness in the Public Accounts Committee? He was subpoenaed by the Minister of Public Works, not bv Mr. Crocket.

The charge or insinuation made by the hon. gentleman was that I had sent for Mr. Loggie to come here to Ottawa to make a proposition to buy a part of this property. Is that not what the hon. gentleman meant to convey to this House? The hon. gentleman knows there is not a particle of evidence that could give a shadow of foundation for a statement like that.

What I wish to state to the House is that Mr. Loggie was brought here by the Minister of Public Works to try and prove that the sawdust wharf was worth $5,000. That was what he was brought here for and when he came here the only way in which he could prove it was to get Mr. Loggie to make an offer-of $5,000 or whatever it was.

He was not brought here, so far as I know, for any such per-pose. It appeared in the evidence that he had said to Mr. Stead that the property, in his judgment, was well worth $5,000, and that he would give more for it, and had made an offer to Mr. Murray for it. That is why the committee subpoenaed Mr. Loggie. I had nothing to do with the subpoena.
But that was all after the hearing of the evidence was started and the case was before the Public Accounts Committee.
Mr. Loggie did not come till after that.

Then, of course, Stead was sent by the department to Log-gie because Loggie had been advised of what he was to do. He was to make this offer in order to help the Minister of Public Works out of the hole on the sawdust wharf; there is mo doubt about that at all. So far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, with all this rascality and robbery and thievery, that is going on in that department, we wanted to have an investigation of that department; we asked for one some time ago. I believe it would have been in the interest of the Minister of Public Works to have allowed that investigation, because it would have either-shown that these charges were quite unfounded or the minister would have had to explain it in a different way, because the people of this country believe that the Minister of Public Works either knows something about all this and is allowing it for the purpose of benefiting his friends or for political purposes, or else is interested in it himself. That is the impression that is going all over this country and the minister has not tried, except for some slight explanation here, to explain these serious charges. The very fact of his being interested in the St. John ' Telegraph,' and awarding to John E. Moore, who had never done any dredging before, contracts that would enable Moore to buy out the St. John ' Telegraph' out of the public treasury without his putting in a dollar of his own, is a disgrace to this country.

There is not a tittle of evidence anywhere that the owners of the St, John ' Telegraph ' paid for it out of money they received for dredging contracts. If the hon. gentleman had thought that was the case, surely the time for him to make these (statements was before the Committee on Public Accounts, and he should have subpoenaed these people to come here.

The hon. gentleman knows that iust at the time these things happened the St. John ' Telegraph ' was changed from a Conservative newspaper to a Liberal paper, supported by the Minister of Public Works, and these contracts were all let at the same time at prices which not one man in the Dominion of Canada believes were fair and upright. 323	'

That was the reputation he had-as close as could be, always looking out for the interest of the government, always cutting down those who had furnished supplies' to the government dredges to the finest possible point. That was the complaint made against him for years under both governments. He was felt to he a safe officer to see that only just bills were paid, and that government interest were protected.
Will the minister explain what his duties were in connection with the government dredges?

His duties were to see that they carried out the different dredging operations laid out for them, to see that they did the most efficient work possible, to keep control of their operations from week to week, and to make a report as to whether they were working satisfactorily or ndt; also to visit the dredges from time to time, to purchase supplies for them, and to send in regular reports to the department. The superintendent of dredging is supposed to be constantly looking after the business of the government dredges. Mr. McCord ock, with that large dredging experience, was a man who I felt could be absolutely trusted to give a fair judgment on the matter, and I asked the chief engineer to send him to Gaspereau for the purpose of looking into the dredging work being done, to consider all the circumstances, and to report whether or not 90 cents per cubic yard was a fair and reasonable price. The hon. gentleman would, I suppose, have it believed by this House that I had in some way influenced Mr. McCordock. Let me say that I had very little personal acquaintance with the late W. J. McCordock, and I had no communication with him on this subject beyond asking him if he could go and visit Gaspereau, and then the communication was with the chief engineer, who gave him his directions in I writing.
Did the minister try at any time to send this gentleman to do this work as government work, when it was so urgent?
I did not, and the reason is that two things are necessary in order to do government dredging: One is to have the superintendent, and the other is to have the dredge.
Did you have them?
No. The dredges were employed in other places.
This was urgent work.
So were the others, and it was impossible to take the dredges from them.
Then this was not so urgent as the others?

The hon. .gentleman has read from Mr. McCordock's report. Let me call your attention to what Mr. McCordock says. After stating what they were doing, he says:
I am of the opinion that from the exposed position of the dredging and the detention from shallow water and the difficulty in getting coal and water from the shore out two miles to the dredge, where it has to remain at anchor in all weather, that the amount of 90 cents named in the tender is a fair rate per cubic yard.
Surely these are considerations which ought fairly to enter into the judgment of a person certifying as to the value of the work. They are considerations which would enter into the judgment of every contractor tendering for the woTk. A contractor looks at many things when tendering.
He looks at the exposed position of the work or otherwise. He makes some soundings for himself usually and learns concerning soundings or borings that have been made. He considers' the quality of the materials to be moved, whether clay, sand or slit, or whether there may be boulders. And a very important question with him is that of a fresh water supply for his dredge and tug, and also the question of the coal supply. He must consider also the question of the distance he has to tow his dredges and barges, both to reach the woTk and to get back into winter quarters after the season is finished. No doubt all these things were taken into consideration, by the Maritime Dredging & Construction. Company, when they tendered at 90 cents for this work. Before we agreed to pay this 90 cents Mr. Scammell, the resident engineer of St. John, a young man who had a good deal of experience under Mr. She-wan, being afterwards in charge of dredging operations for the department, was sent,
at my request, up to- the Gaspereau river for the purpose of looking into conditions and making a report. Let me call attention to what he says. I read, not from the printed copy but from the tiles which, I presume, is the same as my friend has.

October 19th, 1908.

from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), who is a lawyer and a very excellent lawyer, one I would like to have represent me if I had a case in court,-it is all very well for him tc talk about what dredging is worth. Or it is all very well for me to talk about it. But whose judgment is best, the judgment of these gentlemen or the judgment of the engineers, experienced men, who went upon the ground and saw these dredges at work, saw the difficulties under which they were labouring, these unfavourable conditions as to coal and water supply and who knew what dangers this dredging plant was exposed to m case of a storm, being out in the estuary and outside the shelter that would have been afforded could they have got well into the river?

I would like to ask the hon. minister a question. Were not all these things present to the mind of the engineers of the department when they estimated that the dredging could be done at 22 cents a yard?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) must not make a mistake about that. This estimate of 20 cents was made before the work was undertaken at all and was made for work to be done by a government dredge.

I know these things are never taken into account.

They are not. All that is taken into account is the ordinary repairs of the dredging season. Even the large repairs, which in the case of dredges are 'necessary almtost every winter, are not included. The depreciation and wear and tear are not included. No interest on construction is allowed for. The dangers involved in having a dredge in a place like that are not taken into consideration. But ell these things must be taken into consideration by a dredging contractor when he makes a tender for work. My hon. friend from Westmoreland has told us that these contractors lost a tug, wrecked in connection with these dredging operations, and this accident involved a loss of quite a number of thousands of dollars. I have in mind the case of Mr. Connolly who was taking a very valuable dredge from one Mr. PUGSLEY.
part of the Atlantic coast to another and the dredge was wrecked in a storm. The other day at St. Andrews a dredge that was operating under the Dominion Dredging Company, under contract with my department sank through some unexplained reason, and it took a good many days before the dredge could be raised, and it will take a good many days more before its machinery can be put right and the dredge set in operation again. When any expense of that kind occurs, not only is there the loss involved by reason of the wreck itself, but there is also the expense of the crew and the loss on investment. Particularly when a contractor is working in an exposed position he runs the risk of losing his plant or of having it greatly injured. Now, I want to repeat what I stated when this matter was before the House in February, 1910, that you cannot judge what the real, fair value of dredging work in one place is from what it costs in another; you cannot form any fair judgment upon the subject. The contractor would, as I have said, have to take all these conditions into consideration, and then after the work is begun, the engineer going upon the spot would be the man who would be able to form the best conclusion. When the government invite tenders for works, do they not usually have surveys, borings, diagrams, so that they can have an estimate of their own engineers? Was not that done in this instance, or is it the custom of the Public Works Department when they invite tenders for dredging?

I have stated that four or five years before this dredging was done, in 1903, the late Mr. Day was asked to make borings and to make a report. He reported for a channel four feet deep at low tide, and his estimate was that it would be worth 20 cents per cubic yard. I say that frankly, there is no dispute about that. Then later on, in 1908, Mr. Stead appears to have adopted Mr. Day's estimate. What I say is that that is based, I have no doubt whatever, upon what he thought would be the fair cost of doing the work by a government dredge. Then after the work was done, we have Mr. Stead's certificate, and this would show the conditions under which the work was being done, the exposed situation on which this particular work across the bar was being done. He joined with the others, and forwarded these certificates to the department. You may ask me why Mr. Stead changed his mind. Perhaps he was influenced by Mr. McCordock and Mr. Scammell, because it is a matter of judgment. But it is enough for me that, having sent down these two independent officers of the department and the chief engineer, having got their reports that the prices were fair and reasonable, it seems to me I was quite justified in paying the amount of the tender price. But more than that, we have the further proof that in the following year, even upon the inside work, which was less exposed than this work across the bar, the actual cost of the operation of" the government dredge was 41 cents per cubic yard.

I understand the hon. gentleman to say that at the time he asked for tenders for that work, the department did not have sufficient information to give the contractors; the government was going it blind and the contractors were going it blind, and they estimated the work after it was done.

My hon. friend must realize that we would have a rep\,*t showing the rate at which the work would have to be done. It was estimated by Mr. Day for a four foot channel. Of course, any difference between the four feet and the six feet we would not know, the contractor would have to take his chances. Now, let me call attention to a matter in regard to which I would have supposed that my hon. friend would have made a motion before this House, and that is the dredging of. the Miramichi river. When I first became minister and called for tenders for dredging upon the Miramichi river, the lowest tender was for 60 cents per cubic yard. The lowest tenderer was Mr. W. J. Poupore, a gentleman who has devoted a great deal of attention to dredging matters, and no criticism has been made of that contract being awarded to Mr. Poupore. I looked into "the matter very carefully with the thief engineer of my ^department. I called for tenders, and in such a way that we could consider the dredging tender for the horseshoe and bar, and for the Grand Dune flats.
In that case did the minister allow the work to go on preceding the receipt of tenders?
No.
What has that to do with this case?
I expected to get a bouquet from my hon. friend for this,
I am afraid that I could not give it to my hon. friend under any circumstances.
Not under any conditions?

That proves how very shortsighted my hon. friend is.

We called for tenders and. got separate tenders as well as joint tenders for the whole of this work. I would have supposed that my hon. friend, the member for York, would have called attention to this as well as to other matters which could not help appealing to any fair minded man, which could not help almost certainly commanding his approval.

The hon. gentleman heard of it because it was brought to his notice during the session. But if the hon. gentleman were to speak of anything in connection with my department or in connection with myself in terms of approval, I am sure it would arouse astonishment amongst his constituents, and you might hear the remark made upon all sides that suddenly the hon. gentleman had grown to a better manhood .and a bigger intellectual condition than that with which they had hitherto credited him, and it would be a very great surprise.

Mr. Speaker, I shall read again the paragraphs in the Revised Statutes of Canada which ought to govern the conduct of the Minister of Public Works, in the matter with which we have been dealing this afternoon; and I beg most respectfully the attention of this House to the wording of this statute because it is the law defining the obligations of ministers in the conduct of such matters as we are dealing with. The clauses apply not m-erly to the Minister of Public Works, but to the ministers of all departments conducting works on behalf of the public in this Dominion.
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works except in cases,
(a) of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest.

I need hardly say that no such case is pretended to have been in existence or to have been made out. If it were necessary to go further into that at this moment I would be prepared to do so, but I shall not delay the House with it now.
(b)	In which, from the nature of the work, it can he more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
There is no pretence that any such case existed here.
(c)	Where the estimated cost of the work is less than $5,000.
I need not read further because there is no pretence that that case existed.
Whenever, in case of any work, tenders are required to be or are invited, the minister having charge of the department concerned shall submit all tenders received therefor to the Governor in Council, and the contract for tae work shall be awarded under the direction ot the Governor in Council.

Another unfortunate man, the head of a great institution, is n,ow serving time for having evaded his duties under Acts of Parliament. Are we to treat one class of eases differently from another? If these men go to the penitentiary for evading their statutory duties, why should a minister of the Crown be allowed to set at naught the statutes of the country at his sweet will? That is the point we are here to discuss; that is the object of the resolution. The h&n. gentleman has carefully observed that, no doubt, and he has with equal care avoided referring to it.
Now, I propose not to go into outside discussions.
